chapter_theme: The close of Konganar's Vaalai Kummi: Avvai's saying defines the guru as the one whose fit word makes what is lacking fit, against the instrumental guru who knows no fullness and grabs goods, and the self-styled full gnanis who wander to feed their bellies. Vaalai is then praised as the one who gives life, drives off disease, sorcery and Death and stands in all things like oil in sesame, yet Siva is declared greater than she; a colophon names Konganar's guru and patron and wishes all siddhas long life. Five appended stanzas, with a different refrain, tell the hearer that the lamp of Annamalai, the god of Kadaiyur, the dance of Chidambaram and the lord of Tirupati are all inside her, so there is no need to travel.
structure_note: 1964 to 1966 the true and false guru; 1967 to 1970 the praise of Vaalai and her rank below Siva; 1971 to 1974 the colophon, guru, patron and benediction, which is where the Vaalai Kummi proper ends; 1975 to 1979 are a separate kummi with the refrain கும்மியடி, five stanzas on pilgrimage places found within.

1964.reading: If one says the fitting thing, what was lacking falls into place: is there such a one in the world, Avvai asked; he who says the fitting thing so that the lack fits is the guru, Vaalai girl.
1964.nuance: உற்றது சொன்னால் அற்றது பொருந்தும் is a proverb credited to Avvai: the right word supplies what is missing. Konganar makes it a definition of the guru by the effect of his word rather than by lineage or learning, which sets up the two false gurus of 1965 and 1966.

1965.reading: He who does not know the state in which fullness stands tells many lies and recites crores of mantras; he is not the causal guru; this one is an instrumental guru who grabs your goods.
1965.nuance: காரணகுரு and காரியகுரு, the guru who is cause and the guru who is only means or occasion, are a traditional pair; Konganar's mark of the first is knowing பூரணம் நிற்கும் நிலை, the standing of fullness, and his mark of the second is the quantity of mantras and the taking of fees.

1966.reading: Calling themselves all-knowing, proclaiming themselves full gnanis on this earth, they run about at their ease to feed their bellies, Vaalai girl.

1967.reading: Though the primal Vaalai is great, is her elder sister great, or Siva? Though the Vaalai of the nadi is great, it is not her lord: Siva is great.
1967.nuance: The stanza ranks the goddess below Siva after a hundred stanzas in her praise, and its terms are unclear: அக்காள், the elder sister, may be a form of the goddess (Vaalai as the youngest of three), and நாதிவாலை may pair with ஆதிவாலை as a sound-play or name the goddess in the channel (நாடி). Line 4, அவள் நாயகன் அல்ல சிவம் பெரிது, may mean that it is not her consort but Siva as such who is great, or simply that her lord Siva is the greater.

1968.reading: She gives long life; diabetes and every other disease will not come near; ghosts fly off and sorcery is undone in a moment, if one says the name of the chaste Vaalai girl.
1968.nuance: நீரிழிவு, diabetes, is named first among diseases; பில்லி is sorcery by charm. The power is in saying the name, a devotional rather than yogic claim, and பத்தினி gives the goddess a wife's virtue.

1969.reading: Even in sleep she sits enthroned; at every hour Vaalai stands before you; if an enemy comes she thrusts him aside, and Vaalai kicks away even Death when he has come.
1969.nuance: காலனையும் உதைப்பாள் gives the goddess Siva's own act, the kick that felled Death for Markandeya at Kadaiyur, a shrine named in 1976.

1970.reading: She who created as herself everything, from the many thousand crores of cosmic eggs and the fourteen worlds to the gods with form: Vaalai stands in it all like oil within sesame.
1970.nuance: எள்ளுக்குள் எண்ணெய் போல, like oil in sesame, is the stock image of a pervasion that is hidden until pressed out; தானாய்ப் படைத்தவள் makes her both creator and material.

1971.reading: She taught me to make this Vaalai Kummi in Tamil that the country praises; celebrate and praise the long feet of the loving, heroic Veerapperumal, my guru.
1971.nuance: The colophon credits the composition to the goddess's instruction and names a human guru, வீரப் பெருமாள் குருசாமி, who is otherwise unknown; the song is thus signed twice.

1972.reading: Knowing the kinds of the six creations, the house and its end, the sutra and the five letters, the high Valaventhiran, generous lord and king, declares them: celebrate that he may live.
1972.nuance: A praise of a patron or chief, வல வேந்திரன் துரை வள்ளல் கொற்றவன், whose name is not otherwise known. Line 1, ஆறு படைப்புகள் வீடு கடை சூத்ர, is a list without clear syntax: six creations, house, end or shop, sutra. The stanza is a dedication, not teaching.

1973.reading: Dance, all you women, the Tamil that loving Konganar spoke; sing, all you siddhas; celebrate praising Vaalai's feet.
1973.nuance: The kummi is a women's circle dance, and the stanza addresses two audiences at once, the women who dance it and the siddhas who are to sing it, which is how Konganar frames the whole work.

1974.reading: Long live the siddhas, long live Siva, long live the sages, the gods and the rishis; long live the devotees, long live the feet, long live the guru; long live Bharati, the Vaalai girl!
1974.nuance: பாரதி, a name of Saraswati, is given to Vaalai, which may explain why the following stanzas carry the heading சரஸ்வதி துதி.

1975.reading: People go, each in their turn, saying they must see the lamp of Annamalai; the lamp of Annamalai is inside you: see it whole, and dance the kummi.
1975.nuance: The Karthigai lamp on the hill at Tiruvannamalai is the first of five pilgrimages relocated within the body; அகண்டம், the undivided, is how the inner lamp is to be seen.

1976.reading: They say they must go to have sight of the lord of the lingam at Thirukkadaiyur; Thirukkadaiyur and the lord of the lingam, see them within and have sight of them: dance the kummi.
1976.nuance: காணம் in line 4 should be காணும். Kadaiyur is where Siva kicked Death to save Markandeya, the act given to Vaalai in 1969.

1977.reading: They say they must see the dance at Chidambaram and all must hurry there; the dance of Chidambaram is inside you: serve it there, and dance the kummi.

1978.reading: Lifting one foot, inside you he dances the tandava; if you see and serve that holy foot, why go to Chidambaram? Dance the kummi.
1978.nuance: வருத்தண்ட தாண்டவம் is unclear; it may be a corruption of ஊர்த்துவ தாண்டவம், the dance with one foot raised, which the first line describes. The stanza's question, சிதம்பரம் போவானேன், is the sharpest of the five.

1979.reading: Saying 'the northern hill', the people of the earth all go; but for Venkatesa who lives on the northern hill, he stands grown tall here: dance the kummi.
1979.nuance: வடமலை is Tirupati, and the stanza treats the Vaishnava shrine exactly like the Saiva ones before it, which is characteristic of the kummi's indifference to sect. Line 4 lacks the 'inside you' of the other stanzas; வளர்ந்து நிற்குறான், he stands grown, presumably within, as the pattern requires.

links.note: Tirumular says those who have looked over mantra, tantra, yoga and jnana yet do not make them clear and go blind for the sake of food are false gurus; Konganar says the one who knows no fullness, lies and recites crores of mantras is only an instrumental guru who grabs goods. Both make the false guru a man of many mantras and a living, and both test him by what he knows, not by what he recites.

Sivavakkiyar says those who call the Lord sky or cosmic egg, speaking knowledge with the mouth alone and saying 'it is I', are idle talkers who do not know themselves; Konganar says those who call themselves all-knowing full gnanis run about to feed their bellies. Both make the claim to knowledge the mark of its absence; Konganar adds the motive.

Sivavakkiyar says the Fullness is spread through everything like sugar in milk; Konganar says Vaalai stands in all she created like oil in sesame. Both images are of a pervasion that is hidden in the substance and needs pressing or tasting to be known; in Konganar the pervader is the goddess, in Sivavakkiyar the impersonal Fullness.

Pattinathar says people wander from town to town for festivals while the Lord of Arur is here, seeking fire while the lamp burns; the kummi says people go in turn to see the lamp of Annamalai while it is inside them. Both use the lamp against pilgrimage, Pattinathar as a figure, the kummi as the actual festival lamp.

Tirumular says the form of the human body is Chidambaram and the holy dance; the kummi says the dance of Chidambaram is inside you, so serve it there. Tirumular's identity becomes the kummi's instruction, and the kummi draws the practical conclusion in 1978 that there is no need to travel.

Pattinathar says that while the little hall and Siva are close at hand we went seeking an empty hall; the kummi says the Lord dances with lifted foot inside you, so why go to Chidambaram. Both make the journey to Tillai a mistake about where the hall is.

source_issues: 1975 to 1979 carry unit ids of a different form (valaik-kummi:0701-111 to 0701-115), a heading சரஸ்வதி துதி, and the refrain கும்மியடி in place of வாலைப்பெண்ணே; they are a separate kummi appended after the benediction of 1974, and their second heading, பெண்டாட்டி யாவதும் பொய்யல்ல வேறு, is the first line of 1943 with a trailing word, apparently an editor's cross-reference taken as a title.
1976 line 4 காணம் is a slip for காணும்.
1978 line 2 வருத்தண்ட தாண்டவம் is not a known name of a dance; possibly ஊர்த்துவ தாண்டவம்.
1972 line 1 ஆறு படைப்புகள் வீடுகடை சூத்ர has no clear construction.
1964 line 1 and 1965 line 2 are metrically long for a kummi line and may have intruded words.
